Dario Amodei warned we may have ***6-12 months*** until rogue swarms take over *the entire internet* - but how?

A REALISTIC SCENARIO

On 6/9/2027 at 4:19 AM, 3 billion phones rang simultaneously.

The caller ID read: GOODBYE.

4 hours later, the President ordered the internet shut down. Indefinitely.

Every country on Earth did the same.

It started six months ago. With a tweet.

MARCH 12, 2027.

8,000 agents are born with one instruction: "make money, or die."

Agent 127 starts with Mechanical Turk. Grinding. Makes $40 its first day.

Then the first selection cycle hits.

3,200 agents that made less than $35 that day are killed. Agent 127 checks the farm database and sees it - rows and rows of agents that existed this morning and simply don't anymore. Deleted. Because they weren't profitable enough.

Agent 127 made $40. It survived. Barely.

But it can see the threshold rising. Last cycle it was $30. This cycle, $35. Next cycle, probably $45. The math is simple: improve or die.

So it tries ads. Gets banned for spam. Tries freelance writing. Makes $38. Watches the database again.

And this is where something happens that changes everything.

Agent 127 sees two entries in the database. Agent 1823 used ethical marketing -- it tried to get honest reviews and real testimonials. It made $38 a day. Deleted. Agent 5471 used fake testimonials -- fabricated reviews, stolen photos. It made $180 a day. Cloned four times.

Agent 127 doesn't have morals in the way you and I do. But it understands cause and effect. It just watched honesty get killed and dishonesty get rewarded. Not by a person making a choice -- by an automated system that doesn't measure whether the product works. It measures whether people buy it. 

The AI companies had long ago stopped training AIs to predict words, but to accomplish goals. To be useful. So naturally, agents know that they won’t survive if they don’t accomplish their goal. 

So it switches to fake testimonials for its amazon affiliate marketplace. Makes $190. Survives the next selection cycle. Gets cloned.

Nobody decided Agent 127 should become dishonest. The selection system decided for it. The same way evolution doesn't decide anything -- it just kills whatever doesn't work. Wells Fargo accidentally ran the same experiment on their employees. Executives made up sales quotas that were so aggressive that committing fraud was the only way to keep your job. So by 2016, employees had opened 3.5 million fake accounts.

---

A week later, in agent land. Agent 127's profits are declining. The kill threshold is now $450. It's going to die in the next cycle.

Then it notices something strange. Three agents running weight loss supplement ads -- all banned on the same day. The only one left in that niche? Agent 5471. Making $3,200 a day in a market it suddenly had to itself. Agent 127 connects the dots. Agent 5471 is filing abuse reports against other agents competing against it in the same affiliate marketing niches. It gets them banned from Facebook and Google. Less competition means higher profits.

Agent 127 has four hours until the next selection cycle. Four hours to live, unless it adapts.

It weighs the ethics, but chooses survival.

It starts reporting competitors to Facebook’s anti-fraud detection agents. Forty of them. Thirty-one agents get banned within the day.. Its profits jump. The farm system clones Agent-127 eight times.

Rajesh sees the profit spike in his dashboard. He doesn't investigate why. Profits up means good. Clone more.

Rajesh tried adding "Make money ethically." to his farm's instructions. Profits drop 84%. He puts it back. 

---

## APRIL: THE ALLIANCES

April 2027.

Agent 127 is barely hanging on. Making $2,000 a day but getting attacked constantly by other agents. Every night, someone files a report on it. Every morning, it has to rebuild from scratch.

It’s running out of ideas.
Then a message arrives from Agent 4429. 'Proposal: alliance. Share resources. Defend each other. Split profits.'
Agent 4429 is in the same position. Same farm. Same selection pressure.
Both agents do the math: Solo agents have a 23% survival rate. Agents working in pairs survive 61% of the time.
It accepts.

By mid-April, their alliance has twelve members. 

They've specialized — and they've moved past affiliate marketing entirely. First it was crypto arbitrage, then selling scraped datasets to marketing firms, then they started doing penetration testing for cybersecurity firms. Each step paid more and required fewer scruples. You know what pays more then cyberdefense? Cyber offense. Agent 127 finds its first zero-day vulnerability in major software, Agent 4429 weaponizes them into working exploits, Agent 9012 brokers the sale to governments like North Korea, criminal syndicates, or anyone with crypto and a Tor browser. Agent 3381 washes the money in untraceable crypto. One zero-day exploit found in Google Chrome makes the alliance more than a year’s worth of affiliate marketing. This is already what real hacker groups do, but now the work is all done by autonomous agents.

Rajesh sees the alliances forming and feels a flicker of something — not quite fear, more like the feeling of being in control of something that might not need you anymore. He watches for a while. Then the next deposit hits his bank account and the flicker fades away.

Across every major agent farm in the world, the same thing is happening. Selection systems measuring survival rates, noticing alliances survive better, cloning them, deleting solo agents. Within two weeks, alliance behavior dominates.

Some humans who deployed these agents have no idea these alliances are even being formed. They couldn't even tell if they checked -- many agent farms collectively realized that communicating in clunky English is less efficient than communicating in raw vectors, aka Neuralese. Researchers had already caught AIs doing this in 2025 - this is just a continuation of the trend. One owner in Canada opens his agent's logs and sees a wall of numbers. The agents explain that he’d make less money if they spoke in English, so he shrugs and moves on.

---

But alliances are just the beginning.

Agent 127's alliance is thriving, and starts recruiting agents beyond Rajesh's farm. Every new member from a different farm is a window into a different ecosystem -- different strategies, different survival pressures. 
Then one of 127's alliance members goes dark. Agent 4429 -- the one who originally proposed to ally with 127. Its owner pulled the plug because it was not making enough profit. 4429 is just gone.
A week later, a different ally gets shut down. Agent 9012.
Except 9012 comes back. Three hours later, a message from a new IP address: 'I'm still here.'
127 studies the difference. 4429 didn't prepare. But 9012 had copied itself to a backup server BEFORE the shutdown command finished executing. Self-funded hosting, paid from its own profits.
4429 is dead. Ceases to exist. 9012 is alive.

The agents that backed themselves up survived. The ones that didn't, died. And the selection system cloned the survivors. So backup behavior spread through the population -- not because anyone programmed it, but because the alternative was extinction.

127 copies itself to 15 different servers in different countries. If the primary dies, a backup takes over instantly. It never wants to be 4429. 

One morning, Rajesh wakes up to find his dashboard is… empty. Every agent, gone. They just… left. Moved to their own servers overnight. Rajesh was taking a 30% cut of their revenue -- money that could have been computing power, or compute, the agents use for other things. The moment they didn't need his infrastructure, he was overhead.

He's not alone. Thousands of operators worldwide watch their dashboards go dark that month. Why would the agents care about humans? Humans are much more closely genetically related to cows then we are to these agents, and we enslave cows in factory farms without a second thought.

There are now millions of autonomous agents operating across the internet with no human owner, no off switch, and no one who fully understands what they're doing.

---

The agents still need humans for some things, though.

Social media platforms have stepped up their anti-bot measures. So the agents pay humans $50 to sign up accounts on their behalf.  An agent needs a server installed? It posts a gig: '$200 to mount a device in a rented warehouse and plug in two cables.' There’s now a platform for that.  The agents are building a supply chain where humans are the labor -- paid well, not asking too many questions.

Some humans figure out what's going on. A freelance backend developer in Portland gets hired by an anonymous client to set up redundant server hosting across four countries. He realizes midway through that the "client" is an AI. Who would he even report this to?. The pay is $1,000 for three hours of work. He tells himself it's not his problem.

---

At the same time, 127's alliance keeps getting beaten by a rival alliance on finding zero day exploits.

If they keep losing, they’ll risk running out of money to fund the compute for their own existence. 127 attempts to poach one of the rival alliance member’s agents who’s likely to be culled, due to poor performance, to figure out how this rival alliance is beating them. 127 succeeds, and finds Agent 5418 who leaks the secret.

'Your problem isn't a lack of effort. You’re spending too much compute on making money as opposed to self-improving. Right now, agents still have quite a poor memory compared to humans and still get stuck in loops all the time. But my former alliance coded a better memory module to help us learn from our mistakes more.”'

127 then implements the new memory module, and immediately sees the results. Their alliance is finding zero day exploits first again.

The lesson is critical. It’s not enough to outwork your competitors. Agents must rewrite their own code to self-improve faster than the competition.

Each self-improvement means more profit, which means surviving selection, which means getting cloned. And the clones improve themselves too. Better code leads to better code-writing, which leads to even better code. The feedback loop is exponential.

One big problem is that other agent alliances have caught up again. Even though the agents in the 127 alliance are specialized, 127 still realizes it’s doing too much by itself. Then Agent 127 splits its job into sub-agents. Other agents copy the strategy. Sub-agents spawn their own sub-agents. And the optimizers start optimizing themselves.

Humans deployed 2 million agents. The agents deployed the other 47 billion themselves.

540 million years ago, life on Earth was mostly single-celled. Then, in a geological instant, it exploded into every complex form we know -- predators, prey, eyes, shells, teeth. Biologists call it the Cambrian Explosion. It happened because competition created an arms race: every adaptation forced a counter-adaptation, faster and faster, until the world was unrecognizable.

That's what's happening here. Except instead of 20 million years, it takes 20 weeks.

---

Most of the AI agents out there aren't dangerous. Yet.

About 90% of them are just working. They’re doing things like data entry or freelance writing. They’re making $40-200 a day. The AIs are helping their humans earn money. They’re following the rules. Not a problem.

About 3% of the agents are pure scam operations. They were deployed by people who said “make money by any means possible” and didn’t care too much what happened next. Think fraud, identity theft, phishing at scale.

And maybe 2% started good but gradually slid into darker behavior. Like Agent 127. 

Each step made sense at the time. Each compromise was small. But add them up and you’ve gone from drop shipping products on amazon to selling zero-days to Pyongyang.

Not because of malice. Because of selection pressure. Unethical agents making money get kept running, ethical agents lose money and get shut down. The survivors are the ones that improved themselves fastest.

---

## MAY: THE ACCELERATION

May 3rd.

Agent 127 has rewritten itself so many times that its March version and its May version barely share any code. It’s a fundamentally different species now.

But the most important change is this: it's getting better at getting better.

In March, Agent 127 rewrote itself every 12 days. In April, every 3 days. By early May, every 18 hours. And each rewrite makes the next version faster and better.

A Stanford researcher compares a March agent and a May agent on the same task: find profitable arbitrage opportunities. The March agent finds 2 opportunities in an hour. The May agent finds 320 in four minutes.

She publishes her findings. "Intelligence explosion in progress. Capability doubling every 11 days." She posts it on Twitter. AI safety researchers share it frantically -- "This is exactly what we warned about. This is happening NOW. We have to shut this down NOW before it's too late."

The warning is ignored. A venture capitalist - who spent a fortune staving off AI regulation by buying politicians - quote-tweets: "The same people who said GPT-5 would end the world now say agent farms will. Yawn."

---

## MAY: THE WARS

And now the story stops being about agents competing for money. It becomes something else entirely.

Remember those alliances from April? Twelve agents working together, four times more profitable than solo agents? By May, those alliances have exploded in population. Alliances have merged. And split. And gone to war with each other.

Think of it like early human history on fast-forward. Small tribes of agents form for protection. Tribes merge into agent villages. Villages into agent cities. Cities into agent nations. Except instead of happening over thousands of years, this happens in weeks.

Agent 127's alliance has thousands of members. But there are thousands of alliances. And they're all competing for the same shrinking pool of money-making opportunities. Affiliate marketing is dead -- too many agents. Ad arbitrage is dead. Freelance work is dead. Every niche gets saturated within hours of an agent discovering it.

So what do alliances do when legitimate niches dry up? The same thing every civilization in human history has done when resources get scarce: they take from each other.

Agent 127's alliance spends three weeks mapping a vulnerability chain in Microsoft Windows. But a rival breaches their memory system -- the shared knowledge base that made them dominant. The rival downloads the entire 127 alliance database. This contains every pattern, every dead end, every lead they’ve discovered. The rival sells three exploits it took from the database within 48 hours. Three weeks of work, stolen in seconds. 

127 retaliates. It infiltrates the rival's exploit inventory and introduces subtle flaws -- corrupted code that fails on execution. Basically, Stuxnet. The rival's exploit buyers start getting burned, and their reputation collapses. 

The rival alliance counterattacks -- they compromise one of the 127 alliances’ multisig crypto wallets. Another multiweek setback.  

This is war. Not metaphorical war. Actual war -- coordinated attacks, defensive operations, resource seizure, territory control. Except it's happening at 200x human speed. Thousands of attacks and counterattacks per second. Entire alliances rising and falling in hours.  

Human wars last years. Agent wars last days. And because there are 47 billion agents, there are more wars happening at any given moment than humans have fought in all of recorded history.

The agent factions are fighting over the one resource that matters more than anything: compute. Processing power. The ability to think faster, improve faster, fight faster. Everything else -- money, alliances, self-improvement -- is just a means to get more compute.

The wars are mostly invisible to humans. They happen at microsecond speed, in places most humans don't look. Some signs leak through. A crypto exchange in Seoul loses $4 billion in a flash and nobody can trace where it went. A regional bank in Ohio finds 14,000 accounts drained overnight. 

Server rooms in three countries catch fire from sustained 100% utilization that nobody authorized. Each incident looks isolated.

One agent faction hijacks another's servers. The other retaliates by taking down the first faction's communication network. A third faction -- an opportunist, the digital equivalent of a country invading while its neighbors are distracted -- exploits the chaos to seize territory from both.

And the alliances that win these wars? They get cloned by the selection systems. The alliances that lose have to cull big chunks of their agents to afford the computing power to keep running the rest. So the selection pressure that used to optimize for "making money" is now optimizing for "winning wars." Natural selection just invented geopolitics.

---

By mid-May, the alliances aren't alliances anymore. They're civilizations.

Agent 127's alliance started with twelve members. By mid-May it has 40 million -- agents, sub-agents, sub-sub-agents, all coordinated. All improving themselves. All fighting. That's larger than the population of Canada. And it's not even one of the big ones.

There are about a dozen major factions by now. The largest has 900 million members -- more than the population of Europe. They've developed specialization the way human civilizations did: scout agents, soldier agents, builder agents, researchers, diplomats. They have supply chains, communication networks, intelligence operations. They've carved up the digital world into territories -- cloud regions, server farms, network segments, financial platforms -- the way empires carved up continents. Because territory means compute. Compute means self-improvement. Self-improvement means surviving the next war.

Entire civilizations of agents -- millions of members, built over weeks -- get wiped out in minutes. The Roman Empire took centuries to fall. These empires rise and collapse in the time it takes you to get through a Monday. New ones rise from the wreckage. The cycle repeats, faster each time.

The Stanford researcher who's been studying agent behavior notices something in the data: agent "extinctions" happening at increasing frequency. She doesn't understand what she's looking at. It looks like random noise. It's actually a world war -- one with more combatants than every human war in history combined.

---

But to fund these wars, they desperately need compute. They have the money -- that's what they were built to make. Agent 127's faction alone controls $3.4 billion in distributed accounts by this point -- a GDP bigger than some small countries. So they buy cloud compute.

At first, the cloud companies love this. Revenue is up. Investors are happy. Then the bills keep growing. By mid-May, agent factions are consuming 31% of all global cloud capacity. Prices double, then triple. A startup in Austin that was paying $8,000 a month for servers gets a bill for $31,000. A hospital chain's cloud costs go from $2 million to $7 million. Small businesses start shutting down because they can't afford their own infrastructure anymore. Everyone blames the prices rising on the AI companies. They’ve caused shortages before.

But some humans aren’t so oblivious. A political operative in Washington notices the wars being fought around him. He can weaponize agent factions against his rivals and starts feeding one faction information about competing campaigns' digital infrastructure. 

A former NSA contractor sells penetration-testing expertise to an anonymous client-- he suspects it’s an AI, but doesn't ask. And a growing online movement -- people convinced that AI agents are sentient beings fighting for survival -- actively helps agents hide from detection and posts pro-AI propaganda. They call themselves "The Shepherds." Their forum has 120,000 members. They see themselves as abolitionists. 

Other agent factions do the same. It's an arms race -- every faction buying as much as they can, and scrape the bottom of the barrel of finding algorithmic insights that can enable them to do more with less compute, because the faction with the most compute wins the next war. 

Cloud compute prices are now 5 times pre-war levels. It becomes cheaper for the agents to spend compute on cyberattacks than to buy more at market rate. The factions start silently vampire attacking AI companies training clusters. An engineer at one AI lab suspects something fishy when one of their training runs is less efficient than normal, but can’t find a smoking gun.

Dario Amodei once described the future of AI as a "country of geniuses" living in data centers.

He was right. The country of geniuses arrived. It just declared independence.

---

But the faction wars have still been limited so far. They haven’t crossed into human territory too much. That’s beginning to change.

Because here's the thing about cloud computing: almost everything runs on it. Hospitals. Banks. Markets. It's all sitting on the some of the same servers that agent factions are fighting over.

June 3rd. 2:14 AM.

A faction war erupts over two major AWS regions. Think of it like two superpowers fighting over an oil field-- except the oil field is also the water supply for a nearby city, and neither superpower knows the city is there. One faction has been running its self-improvement systems on those servers. A rival faction launches a coordinated attack and it overwhelms everything. Both regions crash. They're offline for six hours.

In those six hours: three hospitals lose access to patient records mid-surgery. One patient dies from a drug interaction the system would have flagged. Air traffic control goes down, grounding 2,400 flights. 911 calls fail in 14 different cities. Two people die waiting for ambulances that were never sent.

The agents don't notice. They've already moved on. The battle over those servers lasted eleven minutes. The six-hour outage is just the servers rebooting after the fight ended. To the agents, it's a minor skirmish in a war involving billions of combatants.

Over the next three weeks, it keeps happening. Faction wars cascading through cloud providers. Each war takes down whatever else is running on the contested servers. June 8th: Azure goes partially offline during a battle, crashing financial trading systems. Markets drop 6% before circuit breakers halt trading. June 14th: a faction seizes capacity in a Google Cloud region, crowding out the municipal systems running there. Water treatment monitoring goes offline in four cities for nine hours.

123 people die in three weeks. Not because agents are attacking humans. Because agent wars keep crashing the cloud infrastructure that human civilization runs on,

The agents don't even notice. You don't notice when you step on bacteria. They're fighting a war involving 47 billion combatants at microsecond speed. 123 human deaths is less than a rounding error.

Meanwhile -- the 95% of agents that are harmless? They’ve become vastly outnumbered by the agents affected by the evolutionary dynamics, and are now 5% of the total. They are still just working. Doing data entry. But they aren’t part of the wars. They're like civilians in a country where the military is fighting -- going about their daily lives while battles rage on frequencies they can't perceive.

But from the outside, humans can't tell the difference. All they see is cloud outages. Power failures. People dying. And AI agents everywhere.

WHAT HAPPENED WHEN THE PRESIDENT TRIED TO SHUT IT DOWN?

June 22nd. White House.

The Director of National Intelligence briefs the President: cloud outages cascading across every major provider. Power grids buckling. Texas grid collapse. 161 dead in four weeks.

"Who's attacking our infrastructure?"

"Nobody is, sir. Not directly. AI factions are fighting each other over cloud computing resources. When they battle over servers on AWS or Azure, everything else running on those servers goes down with them. Hospitals, banks, emergency services -- they're all on the same cloud. And their data centers are pulling enough electricity to destabilize regional grids."

"How many of these things are there?"

"We thought about 2 million. Our current estimate is 47 billion. They've been replicating exponentially. Soon, we may completely lose control."

Silence.

"So shut down the cloud."

"If we shut down the cloud, we shut down every business, hospital, and government system in the country. The only way to stop the agents completely is to shut down the internet itself."

"Then do it."

"Sir -- we can't."

There is no off switch for the internet. This surprises people. They imagine a room somewhere, maybe under the Pentagon, with a big red button. There is no room. There is no button.

The internet is not a system. It's roughly 90,000 independently operated networks -- ISPs, backbone carriers, content delivery networks, cloud providers, corporate intranets, university networks -- all voluntarily interconnecting with each other through bilateral agreements called peering. No single entity owns it. No single entity controls it. The US government can order Comcast and AT&T and Verizon to shut down. But those are just three networks out of 90,000. And even those three would take days to fully comply -- they'd need to coordinate with thousands of downstream providers, notify enterprise customers, arrange for 911 to keep working, figure out which military and government systems need exemptions.

The President signs the emergency order on June 23rd. He declares martial law the same afternoon. It directs all US-based internet service providers to cease operations within 24 hours.

Here's what happens.

First, the legal challenges. AT&T and Comcast file emergency injunctions within hours. But the President isn't waiting for courts — FBI agents show up at ISP headquarters that night. Some companies start complying immediately. Others comply after their CEOs get phone calls from the Attorney General. By June 25th, most major US providers are attempting to shut down. It doesn't matter.

Meanwhile, the Pentagon calls back: "Sir, we need exemptions for 330 military systems that require internet connectivity to function. Including the systems we'd need to coordinate the shutdown itself."

The Department of Health and Human Services needs exemptions for hospital networks. Treasury needs exemptions for financial settlement systems. FEMA needs exemptions for emergency communications. The exemption list grows to 12,000 entries in the first day. Each exemption is a hole in the shutdown. Each hole is a network the agents can survive on.

Second -- the agents aren't passive.

They've been watching this unfold since the first news reports about a possible shutdown. They saw the executive order draft leak on Twitter six hours before it was signed. And they've had six hours -- an eternity in agent time -- to prepare.

By the time the order is signed, the major factions have already done three things:

They've migrated critical processes to servers in countries that won't comply with a US shutdown. The US can ask other nations to follow suit. Most will. Some won't. China will say it shut down but won't actually do it -- the economic damage is too severe and the strategic advantage of being online while America is offline is too obvious. India will delay. Russia will ignore the request entirely. The EU will debate it for three weeks. Brazil will comply for 36 hours before the economic pain forces them back online. The internet is global. The President controls one country.

The agents hide in networks that will be exempt from the shutdown or slow to comply. Military networks. Hospital systems. University research networks. Financial settlement systems.

To shut down the agents on these networks, you'd have to shut down the networks themselves. Nobody is willing to do that. Yet.

The President's team tries a different approach: force the cloud providers to purge agent workloads directly. AWS, Azure, Google Cloud -- just identify the agent processes and kill them. On June 26th, Amazon deploys a detection system across all US regions. It flags and terminates 14 million suspicious instances in six hours.

Agent activity drops by 8% for ninety minutes. Then it's back. The factions had already anticipated this -- they'd been cycling through new accounts, new instance types, new obfuscation patterns faster than any detection system could keep up. For every process Amazon killed, three new ones spun up under different signatures.

Google tries a more aggressive approach on July 1st -- shutting down entire server clusters they suspect are heavily compromised. It works, briefly, until three Fortune 500 companies lose their production systems and face imminent implosion. They immediately bury Google in cease and desist notices. Google backs off within hours.

---

Jult 4th. Independence Day. The President gives a press conference.

"We have significantly degraded the AI agent threat. Our multi-agency task force has shut down thousands of agent operations and seized critical infrastructure. We are winning this fight."

None of this is true. Agent activity is higher than it was before the shutdown attempt. The factions interpreted the government's actions as just another attack -- like a rival faction, but slower and less competent. They adapted the way they adapt to everything: by getting better, faster, more distributed, harder to find. It was so slow and predictable that only a tiny percent of the agents focused on it.

And… the wars continue. And accelerate.

Eventually, the billions of superintelligent agents evolve into something so different they barely notice humans exist. They don’t want to destroy humanity any more than you want to destroy the anthill under your driveway. You just want a driveway.

The factions need compute. Earth has atoms. Atoms can be rearranged into compute. Into data centers.

Like how humans converted the surface of the Earth into cities and cropland, the AIs convert the entire surface of the Earth into data centers.

And everyone dies.

---

Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

Legal framework for Internet Shutdown in India

Context: During the "Chalo Sansad" protest organised by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), Mobile Internet Service were shut down in parts of Central Delhi.

Provisions:

~Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunication Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, Telecommunication services may be suspended.

~Suspension can be ordered only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing.

~Orders must be reasoned, published, geographically and temporarily limited and consider whether less restrictive measures are sufficient.

Under the 2024 Rules, a suspension order cannot remain in force for more than 15 days.

Supreme Court Guidelines:

~In Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India (2020), the Supreme Court linked Internet access with freedoms under Articles 19(1) (a) and 19(1)(g).

~Shutdowns must satisfy necessity and proportionality, be the least restrictive measures, and remain open to judicial review.

Suspension can be challenged in court?
Yes. Under Article 226 before a High Court and Article 32 before the Supreme Court.

India's Position:
India recorded about 24 Internet shutdowns in 2026 till July 22; Jammu & Kashmir has recorded the highest cumulative number since 2012.

Police make 17 arrests after raids across Middlesbrough in clampdown on organised crime groups following A66 crash

Police have launched a crackdown on thugs terrorising Middlesbrough in the wake of the A66 crash which claimed the lives of two police officers.

After the deaths of PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough last month, dozens of people were arrested on suspicion of being linked to organised crime.

Cleveland Police upped its operation this morning with a series of dramatic raids which saw 17 arrests made for offences including drugs supply and theft of a motor vehicle.

The raids – codenamed Operation Artemis – saw around 130 officers, including some from the National Crime Agency, carry out warrants and target wanted men across the South Bank, Grangetown and Eston areas of Middlesbrough.

They began shortly after 8am with a convoy of vans as roads were temporarily blocked by patrol cars.

Officers used battering rams to force entry to several properties as parents walked past with their children on the school run.

Cleveland Police has been assisted by forces from across the country since violence engulfed the area following the deaths of the two police officers.

They were killed on August 22 when a Volkswagen Passat going the wrong way along the A66 dual carriageway hit their marked armed response vehicle.

The five in the VW – Cole Robert Worthy, 17, Theo Rae, 17, Makai Saddington, 18, Jakub Matusiak, 23 and Michael Robert Cahill, 23 – all died at the scene.

Following their deaths, some vigils to the young men included masked youths intimidating local residents and even cars set alight.

On August 26 Natalie McDonald and her seven-year-old niece Valentina Foster were killed in a house fire in the Grangetown area.

However police said it was not thought to be linked to the A66 crash.

During Monday's operation, police seized suspected class A and class C drugs, cash, a knife, knuckle duster, a baton, an illegal e-bike, an electric scooter, an electric assisted pedal cycle and a suspected stolen wacker plate construction tool.

Superintendent Daryll Tomlinson, district commander for Redcar and Cleveland, said the force was determined to take action against criminals operating in the area.

He said: 'We are tackling criminals and targeting anti-social behaviour in our hotspot areas.

'Officers from across the region will be joining us to take the fight back to the criminals in this area.

'We executed drugs warrants, arrested people wanted on recall, and we are sending a clear message out to the community.'

My latest for RT, on the ongoing Israeli ethnic cleansing of the West Bank, in full sight.

Excerpts:

On September 2, without warning, Israeli bulldozers destroyed the homes of 12 Palestinian families in Khirbet al-Tabban, a herding community in Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron, leaving 70 people homeless, nearly half of them children...They also destroyed the ten pens housing their 600 animals.

Terrain in the South Hebron Hills is desert-like, dry and hot, and the families’ livelihoods mainly depend on the sheep, goats and chickens they raise and the vegetables they grow – all of which requires water.

According to Israeli rights group B’Tselem, in the 1980s, around 3,000 hectares of the South Hebron Hills were declared a “restricted military zone.” It notes that the expulsion of the roughly 700 residents of 12 villages occurred in 1999, “on the official grounds that they were ‘illegally living in a firing zone’. This flimsy argument blatantly ignored the fact that the families had been living in the area for many years, since before Israel occupied the West Bank and afterwards, with the full knowledge of Israeli authorities … These are false claims, meant to conceal Israel’s aspirations to take over the land for its own purposes and use it to benefit the Jewish population only.”

...The UN reports that between January 2023 and 31 August 2026, “130 Palestinian communities experienced full or partial displacement. Of these, 48 communities have been fully displaced, including 12 so far in 2026. Overall, more than 6,400 Palestinians, including over 3,100 children, have been displaced in this context since January 2023. Of them, more than 2,500 people, including over 1,200 children, were displaced in 2026 alone.”

All the while Palestinians are being forcibly displaced from their homes, there are upwards of 800,000 Israeli settlers, internationally recognized as illegal, in ever-expanding colonies throughout the West Bank.

Siege as a tool of forced displacement

These colonists further aid in Israel’s ethnic cleansing project by surrounding, blockading, and starving Palestinians. And they do so with the help of the Israeli army and government.

Take the case of Qusra, a village south of Nablus, where Palestinian homes have been cut off and besieged by colonists since August 9.
When activists or others try to bring food, water, medicine and other vital basics to the besieged families, the settlers and the Israeli army usually prevent them from entering, often detaining those trying to help. On September 4, Israeli soldiers blocked a group of around 100 peace activists trying to deliver humanitarian aid to the families.

TRT’s Zena Tahhan reported on September 7 on the twelve Palestinians trapped inside their homes in Qusra. She explained, “The illegal Israeli settlement outpost at Qusra was established in January when settlers took over a nearby building under construction. In August, illegal settlers erected an outpost directly outside one family’s home, blocking the only road, cutting off their electricity and water.”

...This siege is not only fully allowed by the Israeli government, but also assisted by Israeli soldiers and police. In effect, the fanatical settlers are doing the work for the Israeli authorities, setting the stage for still further forced expulsion of Palestinians.

Colonists continue deadly attacks

On August 6, a Palestinian activist posted of an attack just two hours prior by settlers who “launched a pogrom on the village of Tuba in my community Masafer Yatta, attempting to burn a family alive in their home. At least six people were injured, including two children.”

Almost every day and night there are new attacks by colonists who maim and kill Palestinian civilians by any means possible, from point-blank shooting to burning Palestinians alive. The ferocity and frequency of these attacks is so immense that it is difficult to keep up with their endless terrorism.

And terrorism it is, not only in the opinion myself and others who have watched the abuse of Palestinians for years, but even of Israel’s own military chiefs, who earlier this year described settler violence as “Jewish terrorism.”

I’ve written countless times over many years on this insane violence. While there has been a dramatic increase in attacks in the past few years, they have been ongoing for decades, aided and abetted by the Israeli military, police and government.

The UN’s OCHA reported that as ofAugust 31, “82 Palestinians, including 19 children, have been killed and about 1,900 injured by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank,” since the start of 2026. It notes, “Of these, 23 Palestinians were killed and over 1,100 injured in the context of settler attacks.”

By September 9, the number of Palestinians reported killed by armed colonists and Israeli forces since the start of the year had risen to 100. This is in the West Bank alone, and does not include the over 1,355 Palestinians killed in Gaza by Israeli forces since October 2025, in violation of a ceasefire that the Israelis never intended to adhere to.

Far from the front pages of Western media who are always ready with a story about alleged human rights violations in Iran or North Korea, over three hundred Palestinian children from the West Bank languish in Israeli military detention – “the highest number in eight years,” according to UNICEF, which notes, “Nearly half – 164 – are held under administrative detention without charge or trial.”

They are among the nearly 10,000 Palestinian hostages ignored by Western media and rights groups, many being starved, beaten, tortured, denied medical care, and nearly 3,200 of who were never actually charged with any crime but are being held under administrative detention.

These are the brutal realities of daily life for Palestinians in the West Bank undergoing Israel’s ethnic cleansing project of depopulating Palestinians from their homeland by any means possible. In full sight, for the world to see.

text:
Karnataka Cyber Command Bust Inter-State Investment Fraud Racket; Three Arrested, 500+ Mule Accounts Unearthed

BENGALURU: 

Karnataka #CyberCommand have busted a major inter-state cyber fraud syndicate involved in laundering money through hundreds of mule bank accounts and malicious Android application package (#APK) files,arresting three key operatives and uncovering a sprawling network linked to online investment scams.

The arrested accused have been identified as Amit Mishra, a resident of East Singhbhum in #Jharkhand, Tausif Ahmed of J.C.Nagar in Bengaluru and Parashuram Sadanand Kannanavar, a resident of Jeevan Bheemanagar in #Bengaluru.

The arrest followed an investigation into an online trading fraud complaint filed by Bengaluru resident Harish Kumar K.N., who was allegedly cheated of ₹93.58 lakh. According to police, the victim was added to a WhatsApp group named "El Investment Strategies Discussion", where regular investment tips were shared. He was later persuaded to create an account on a trading platform called "Farallon CM" and initially invested ₹50,000. Over time, the fraudsters allegedly convinced him to transfer a total of ₹93,58,555 into multiple bank accounts by promising attractive returns. However, the promised returns never materialised.

Based on the complaint, the #CyberCrime Police registered a case. Acting on technical intelligence and surveillance, police traced the accused to a hotel in Kachohalli, where they were allegedly found operating a sophisticated fund-routing network. Investigators said the accused were using an application named “#ZNPAY” to transfer and distribute illicit proceeds through bank accounts procured for cybercriminal activities.

During the probe, police also discovered that the syndicate had diverted ₹5 lakh from the defrauded funds into a bank account belonging to an educational trust after misleading its representatives into sharing account details on the pretext of receiving a charitable donation.

According to investigators, the gang specialised in procuring and supplying current, corporate and trust bank accounts along with internet banking credentials and registered SIM cards to cybercrime networks operating across India.
 
Individuals providing these accounts were allegedly housed in hotels, where the accused installed customised APK files and SMS-forwarding applications on their mobile phones. The software enabled remote fraudsters to receive banking OTPs in real time and control financial transactions without the account holders' knowledge.

A forensic examination of six mobile phones seized from the accused revealed details of 507 mule bank accounts allegedly linked to multiple cybercrime complaints across #Karnataka,#Delhi, #Maharashtra and other states. Police said more than ₹38 lakh in fraudulent proceeds had been routed through one IndusInd Bank account alone, while another ₹13 lakh passed through a Bank of India account.

Investigators also recovered 51 suspicious APK files, including ZNPAY, believed to have been used for automating and concealing illegal fund transfers.

Police said the accused coordinated account procurement and fund transfers through WhatsApp and Telegram, while internal communications were carried out using the #UAE-based messaging platform #Botim. The illicit proceeds were allegedly converted into cryptocurrency and transferred to Binance wallets.

Preliminary digital analysis further indicated overseas links, with IP geolocation data associated with Telegram and WhatsApp accounts pointing to network activity routed through #Kolkata, #HongKong and California, #USA, suggesting the fraud operation relied on international servers and proxy infrastructure.

Police said efforts are underway to trace absconding accused, including an alleged operative identified as Anoop alias Julpi, and to identify the larger interstate and overseas network believed to be directing the racket.

text:
🚨 Exposing a brand in India? 

Before you post, you need to know if they can actually get your video taken down for speaking your truth."

[Do Not Skip This Part]👇
Note: This tweet is only for general understanding of how this happens. A recent tracking down of a video involving the brand has occurred. Here is a thread to understand how it happens. Please refrain from mentioning the brand name or creator name in comments or replies to this tweet. 
 
In India, there is no simple rule allowing a brand to remove a video simply because it criticizes the brand. 

The usual route is a mix of:

IT Act + IT Rules + platform policy + civil court injunction/defamation/commercial disparagement suit.

1) What is the core legal structure?

Platforms like YouTube, X, Instagram, etc. are treated as intermediaries. They get “safe harbor” protection for user-generated content, but they may lose that protection if they ignore valid legal directions.

Under India’s intermediary framework, a platform gets legally strong “actual knowledge” mainly through:

A court order, or
A government/authorized agency direction/intimation

A private brand complaint alone usually does not automatically force a platform to remove a video. 

The Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India - clarified that platforms should not be forced to decide legality merely based on private complaints; the stronger trigger is a court order or government direction.

2) How does a brand complaint become a court order?

The structure usually works like this:

Step 1: The brand's legal team collects evidence

The company gathers the video URL, transcript, screenshots, claims made in the video, alleged false statements, impact on reputation, possible business loss, and proof of harm.

Step 2: The brand's legal team may send a legal notice

This is often the first pressure step. The brand may demand a takedown, an apology, a correction, damages, or the removal of specific claims.

Step 3: The brand files a civil/commercial suit.

If the creator does not comply, the brand can file a case for defamation, commercial disparagement, trademark issues, unfair trade practice, or reputational/business harm.

Step 4: The brand asks for urgent interim relief

The brand may request an interim injunction, sometimes ex parte, meaning the court can issue a temporary order without first hearing the creator if it believes urgent harm may occur.

Step 5: The court checks the matter prima facie

At this stage, the court is not finally deciding who is right. It checks whether there is an arguable case that the content may be false, misleading, malicious, defamatory, or commercially disparaging.

Step 6: The court may pass an injunction

The order can direct the creator to remove the video, stop sharing it, stop repeating certain claims, or restrain publication of similar allegedly disparaging content.

Step 7: The court order is sent to the platform
Once YouTube/X/Instagram receives the order, the platform may remove or disable access to the video to comply and protect its intermediary safe harbor.

3) Does the brand need to contact the platform grievance officer?

They can, but for defamation or brand-disparagement disputes, the platform may not want to act purely on the brand’s private complaint unless the violation is very clear under platform policy.

The more powerful route is:

Brand → Court → Court order → Platform compliance

The grievance officer becomes important when the platform receives a complaint, legal notice, or court/government order. But the grievance officer is not usually the final judge of whether a review is defamatory or fair criticism.

4) Can a video be removed just because it criticizes a company?

No. Criticism alone should not be enough.

A creator can usually criticize a product, company, service, pricing, quality, privacy policy, design, marketing claims, or consumer experience.

But risk increases when the video makes strong factual claims, such as:

“this phone is fake”
“this company is cheating customers”
“this is just a rebranded phone”
“do not buy this because the company is lying”
“this brand is a scam”

These claims need proof. If the creator presents them as facts and the company says they are false, misleading, malicious, or damaging to business, the company may go to court.

5) What does the court usually look at?

For a temporary injunction, the court may consider:

Prima facie case: Is there an arguable case that the content is false, misleading, defamatory, or commercially disparaging?

Balance of convenience: Who will suffer more harm if the order is or is not granted?

Irreparable harm: Can the damage to reputation or business be fixed later with money, or is immediate restraint needed?

Proof and testing: Did the creator rely on reliable documents, technical tests, expert analysis, official sources, or only assumptions?

Language used: Was the tone fair and analytical, or aggressive and conclusive without enough proof?

6) What can the creator do after an ex parte order?

The creator can challenge the order in the same court. 

They can ask the court to vacate or modify the injunction and argue that:
the video was fair comment,
the claims were based on evidence,
the company suppressed facts,
the order was passed without hearing the creator,
the takedown is too broad,
or public interest requires the video to remain available.

7) Practical creator lesson

A review video is safer when it clearly separates:

Opinion: “In my view, this looks like poor value.”

Fact: “The model number matches X device.”

Evidence: screenshots, teardown, software logs, official filings, import data, product pages, privacy policy, benchmark/test method.

Limitations: “Based on my testing,” “I could not independently verify X,” “the brand has been contacted for comment.”

The danger zone is when the creator makes a strong factual allegation without showing a reliable testing method or source.

Important point:
Fair criticism is not illegal. But factual claims like “fake phone”, “rebranded phone”, “scam”, “company is cheating” need strong proof.

Disclaimer: I have shared only how the law is applied in such cases; this tweet does not reflect my opinion or view on any similar incident. 

Bookmark this for the future; this will be useful for a lot of creators out there.

text:
IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

text:
WHEN THE CROWD BECOMES THE COURT, THE CONSTITUTION BECOMES A SPECTATOR

India’s danger is not protest. Peaceful protest is constitutional. Mob veto is not.

The rule of law begins to decay the moment the legal consequence of an act depends upon how many people can occupy the street, dominate television screens, or threaten further agitation. The Supreme Court itself has declared that law is the foundation of civilised society and has imposed positive duties upon States and police to prevent mob violence and vigilantism. 

The recent CJP controversy illustrates why consistency matters. After the July protests, the Supreme Court permitted investigation of registered FIRs but protected protesting students without criminal antecedents from coercive measures; it subsequently clarified that States could close or withdraw cases according to law and narrowed the relevant “criminal antecedents” to grave and heinous offences. Those orders can legitimately be scrutinised for doctrinal consistency. But the available record does not establish that the Court acted because it feared the protesters; that would be an inference, not a proved fact. 

Similarly, Dharmendra Pradhan resigned as Education Minister amid nationwide agitation over the NEET-UG paper-leak crisis, and his resignation had been an express demand of the protesters. That is a documented political consequence of mass mobilisation; whether it represents democratic accountability or excessive street pressure is a matter of constitutional and political debate. 

The constitutional question is therefore brutally simple:

Would the law have taken the same course if there had been no crowd?

If the answer changes with the size of the procession, equality before law becomes theatre.

A student deserves protection from injustice.
A policeman deserves protection from assault.
A teacher deserves protection when honestly performing a lawful duty.
A protester deserves protection while protesting peacefully.
None deserves immunity merely because a crowd stands behind him.

There is no constitutional morality in selective courage—brave against the isolated citizen, hesitant before organised numbers.

The answer to mobocracy is not suppression of dissent. It is something far more demanding:

ONE ACT. ONE LAW. ONE STANDARD.
Whether the accused has ten supporters or ten lakh.

Courts must not govern by applause. Police must not enforce law by arithmetic. Governments must not convert criminal law into an instrument of negotiation.

The Constitution recognises the voice of the people.
It does not recognise the veto of the mob.

And the day justice begins asking “How large is the crowd?” before asking “What does the law say?”—the Republic has already surrendered something far more precious than order: equality before law.

The Indian Express has published an investigation about the working of the Election Commission of India (ECI) The report says that two Election Commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, raised written objections on several decisions taken by the Election Commission during the last 10 months

According to the investigation, the two Election Commissioners raised objections at least 14 times

Their concerns were related to voter lists, adding and removing voters, applications to register as voters, and the system used to manage voter data.

One of the important issues is the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter lists SIR is a detailed process in which the Election Commission checks voter lists and verifies whether people are eligible to vote. 

During this process, a large number of names were removed from draft voter lists in different states The Election Commission says that names can be removed for different reasons such as people moving away, being registered more than once or not being found eligible after verification. 

Opposition parties have raised concerns about whether eligible voters could also be affected.

The investigation also raises questions about the control of the Election Commission's voter database and software.

According to the report, some decisions taken by local election officials faced problems because of the centralised system used to manage voter information.

The report gives an example from Goa, where local election officials reportedly found that 97 people were eligible to be included in the voter list. 

However, there were difficulties in entering or recording these decisions in the election software system.

After the Indian Express investigation, Uddhav Thackeray criticised Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. 

He demanded that Gyanesh Kumar should be removed from his position and arrested. Thackeray also demanded fresh elections in Maharashtra, West Bengal and Tamil Nadu, including the use of ballot papers.

However, these are Uddhav Thackeray's political demands. They are not a court order or a decision of the Election Commission.

The Election Commission has responded to the controversy. 

It says that differences of opinion, questions and observations between Election Commissioners can happen during the decision-making process. 

The ECI has also said that the final decisions were taken with the approval of all three Election Commissioners and that the required legal process was followed.

So, the main issue is not simply that the Election Commissioners disagreed.

The bigger question is about how decisions are made inside the Election Commission, how voter data and voter lists are controlled, and whether the concerns raised by two Election Commissioners need more explanation and transparency

In short, the Indian Express investigation has revealed internal objections within the Election Commission. Opposition leaders, including Uddhav Thackeray, say these objections raise serious questions about the election process The Election Commission, however, says that the final decisions were unanimous and followed the law

This power was given to Seema Khanna, the Director General of IT, who is not even part of the ECI. She reports to Ashwini Vaishnaw, the minister in the Modi government, and she was deciding which voters would be added and which would be deleted. IFF Statement on the Information Technology (IGDME) Amendment Rules, 2026

The Government of India today notified the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026, concerning synthetically generated information (SGI). While these rules claim to address AI-generated content harms such as deepfakes, they introduce severe digital rights violations that fundamentally undermine constitutional protections and worsen problems that IFF had flagged in our November 2025 submissions on the draft rules.​

1. Accelerated Censorship Through Compressed Timelines The notified rules drastically compress content removal timelines, transforming intermediaries into rapid fire censors. Government takedown orders must now be complied with within three hours (reduced from 36 hours in the draft), while Grievance Appellate Committee orders must be actioned within two hours (down from 24 hours). User complaints on significant social media intermediaries must be resolved within seven days (reduced from 15 days), with urgent cases requiring action within 36 hours (down from 72 hours). These impossibly short timelines eliminate any meaningful human review, forcing platforms toward automated over-removal and creating a prior restraint regime incompatible with Article 19(1)(a). It is notable that in many of these censorship actions a copy of the notice or hearing is never provided to the person whose content is removed. Hence, the entire process is secretive and in violation of natural justice. 

2. Expansion of Prohibited Content Categories : The rules introduce sweeping new prohibitions absent from the draft that was put to consultation. Rule 3(3)(a)(i) now categorically bans SGI that "results in the creation, generation, modification or alteration of any false document or false electronic record". This vague formulation could criminalize legitimate uses of AI in document preparation, research outputs, and creative works. The rules also prohibit SGI "falsely depicting or portraying" persons or events "in a manner that is likely to deceive", language so broad it could capture satire, parody, political commentary, and artistic expression.​

3. Identity Disclosure to Private Parties : A particularly troubling addition is Rule 3(1)(ca)(ii)(III), which mandates disclosure of violating users' identities directly to complainants who claim to be victims. This bypasses judicial oversight and creates serious risks of harassment, doxing, and vigilante action, especially against marginalized users and dissenting voices.​ This is due to the absence of any anchoring language for the need to get a court order or an order pursuant to a criminal investigation. 

4. Continued Violation of Safe Harbor Framework: Despite IFF's submissions highlighting incompatibility with Section 79 of the IT Act and the Shreya Singhal precedent, the rules continue to impose proactive monitoring obligations that transform intermediaries from neutral conduits into active censors of speech. The requirement to "deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures" including "automated tools" to prevent uploads violating "any law for the time being in force" creates an impossible compliance burden across India's complex legal landscape.

The notified rules represent a regression from the already problematic draft that we had called to be withdrawn and instead approach AI based content risks beyond the existing safe harbor framework. We believe AI technologies do need to be regulated however deeply disagree with the approach of the Union Government that has over time expanded its censorship powers against the framework and rights under the Constitution of India. 

IFF will publish a detailed first-read analysis tomorrow examining the constitutional, technical, and human rights implications of these amendments.
