People had lots of questions about my drowning child tweet yesterday - eg do I believe in infinite moral obligation? Rather than try to answer piecemeal, I'll just give my whole theory of morality and charity here so you can criticize it or let me know if it has unexpected horrible implications.

I think it's virtuous to help others, including strangers, foreigners, and whichever animals are conscious.

I don't think you have an obligation to do this. I think the word "obligation" should be reserved for explicit or implicit promises. You're obligated to pay back debt, because you explicitly promised to do so. You're obligated to take care of your kids, because you accepted an implicit promise to do so by giving birth to them. You're obligated to follow the law, because of the implicit social contract.

This is a really weak sense of obligation! It's not even clear you're "obligated" in this sense to save the literal drowning child in front of you! I endorse this view - who obligated you to help them? When did you promise it?

So I think in most things we should strive towards some level higher than simple obligation. Let's call this "virtue"*. As a parent, you're obligated to feed and clothe your kid and not abuse them. But to be a virtuous parent, you need to do more - love them, get to know them as a person, go to their soccer games, etc. 

For me the difference between obligation and virtue is that if you fail an obligation, you should be punished by either legal consequences or social opprobrium. If you fail at being virtuous, then . . . I don't know, maybe your close friends should take you aside in private and remind you that you can do better, and if you tell them to shut up, they should drop the issue until they think you're ready to hear it.

The bar for virtue isn't infinitely high. You can be a good parent by supporting your kid and going to soccer games, but you don't have to sell your beloved gold watch which is the only memory of your dead grandfather just so you can buy your kid a slightly shinier soccer ball. Where should the bar be set? I don't think The Moral Law (TM) has any specific answer, but for purely practical reasons I would set it at a place that's just slightly above where you would land otherwise - high enough that you have to work for it, but not so high that it's obviously out of reach and you'll never get there and you should just give up.

I think it's virtuous in this sense to try to help others. What's the bar? I think a natural one is "give between 1% and 10% of your income to a really well-thought-out charity, or something else approximately equally effortful" - but I'm not attached to that. I would actually be okay with ANY careful thought process that ends in a specific nonzero commitment that you're willing to defend, even if that commitment is 0.1%, or an hour a month in a soup kitchen, or whatever.

(but be careful - when you die and go to Heaven, the exact number you pledged will appear on your forehead in gold ink forever)

This obviously doesn't require your to sacrifice your family, or to work yourself ragged, or to give up all hope of a happy life. It's about the same percent of income as the average smoker spends on cigarettes.

Why am I satisfied with so low a bar**, when an even higher bar could save even more people? A couple of reasons (sorry, I keep trying to write this part in a way that doesn't sound like a lecture, and failing, so here's the lecture):

First, 1 - 10%, spent effectively, is enough to save the world. Total American household income is $20 trillion, so if every American donated 1%, that's $200 billion/year. That's about twice as much as PEPFAR + all other foreign aid + all Gates Foundation donations + all other billionaire philanthropy + all effective altruist donations combined. If everyone donated 10%, it would be 20x as much as all of those things combined. I can't say with certainty that there would be no problems left in the world at this rate - but I think we would have cleared a floor of getting rid of the ones that money can quickly solve. Granted that in reality not everyone will give this amount, I still think it's a useful thought experiment in where to set the bar so that you're doing "your share".

Second, the overwhelming majority of your impact comes not from how much you donate, but from how thoughtfully you spend it. Toby Ord thinks that the best charities do 10,000x more good than the worst; if you picked two random charities, on average one would be 100x more effective than the other. If someone donated 100% of their income to an average charity, nobody could claim they weren't doing enough. But by donating 1% of your income to a great charity, you do more good than that person. You can 80-20 this by donating to whoever's at the top of GiveWell's Top Charities leaderboard this year. Or if you have more time you can double-check their work and form your own opinions. 

Third, I'm emphasizing the "sit down, think about it, and make a commitment, however small" aspect, because I think most people already want to be moral, they're just kind of haphazard and thoughtless about it. If an angel presented you with two paths, one of which you spent 100% of your resources on yourself forever, and the other you spend 99% of resources on your self but spent the occasional dollar or hour-of-volunteer-time doing good, and you could just choose one and the angel would make sure that circumstances conspired to make it happen, I think almost everyone would choose the second. They might even try to get the angel to upsell them - "Only 1%? Do you have anything better on offer?" If people fail to give 1% to charity - and most people do - I think it's out of a failure to achieve their own preferences, the same as a scatterbrained person who doesn't file their taxes on time and gets hit with a pointless penalty. When I tweet, I pick on the rare people who insist openly that they really don't care about foreigners, but I think even they are mostly missing some kind of self-knowledge - maybe trying to repress their caring in order to avoid what they fear would be infinite obligation and personal/social misery. If they could prove that they had some sort of crystalline logical omniscience and utterly in the most profound sense didn't care, I would shrug, tell them they were weird, and leave them alone. I talk more about this at https:// www. astralcodexten .com /p/everyones-a-based-post-christian

Fourth, the bar should be wherever it's most useful. Reality has no bar; you can just keep doing more forever. If you devote 99% of your time/energy/money to parenting, you can always ask yourself whether you're failing your kid by not giving 100%. If it's 100%, why not skip sleep and use the time gained to prepare extra-special advanced lesson plans for your home schooling pod? But obviously this will drive you crazy and won't be good for you OR your kid. So in practice, we set a bar as a sort of social technology to encourage low-performers to do better and remind high-performers not to kill themselves. As I said before, the best place for the bar is somewhere where it will serve as inspiration (because it's attainable with more effort) rather than discouragement (because then you know you'll never reach it so why bother). I think 1-10% is a good place to put this.

Isn't it still true that there are people suffering horribly, and if you do one unit more work than the bar, you can always save an extra person? Yes. Effective altruists didn't make this true, and dunking on us on Twitter won't make it stop being true. It's a brute fact about the world. I don't think any moral system can handle it, and ours is no exception. But I think we do a better job than most of staring at the abyss, acknowledging that it's very scary and abyssal, and then trying to do good work regardless. I'm not a Christian, but one thing I admire about Christianity is that it admits we'll all fall impossibly short of moral perfection no matter what we do, then tells us to shut up and get to work being decent people anyway. It even grants us permission to be happy while we're working at it (except for Calvinism, I guess)***. I think effective altruism does better than most other philosophies (possibly excepting some of the really good sects of Judeo-Christianity, which are also excellent at this!) at getting charitable work out of people, while equalling them on how happy and meaningful its adherents' lives are. If you don't have a better alternative, then I think criticizing us for not solving the unsolveable abyss at the heart of everything is unproductive.

The opposite question from the other direction would be - if you don't have an obligation to do charity, why should you do it at all? I think the answer here is the same as "if you don't have an obligation to go to your kids' soccer game, why do it at all?" Ideally you do it out of love. If you don't feel love, you do it out of some sense that it's part of being a dignified well-rounded human and you endorse it in some kind of aesthetic sense even if you don't feel the emotions at this exact second.

If you can't find any sort of generalized compassion instinct anywhere, and you don't share the intuition that it's more rational/dignified/human to be altruistic than not, then (as long as you at least have normal human feelings towards your family members) I suggest trying to have kids. I'm not a very emotional person myself, but having kids gave me a really strong sense of what it is to love someone really really hard. Then I think about the fact that a bunch of kids are dying of preventable diseases in India or wherever, that they have parents just like me, and that those parents would feel just as devastated if their kids died as I would feel if mine did. I don't like thinking about this too much because it's a good way to send yourself into a horror-depression spiral, but being able to think like this when needed helps restrain my natural tendency to end up as one of those guys tweeting stuff like "why save African children when they barely contribute anything to GDP?". If you still don't feel capable of compassion/altruism, try reading the classics. If that doesn't work, try MDMA. If it still doesn't work, then you've tried your best, I excuse you from trying further, and you can give up and get a job at A16Z.

Answers to common questions:

(1) ISN'T THERE A BIG DIFFERENCE BETWEEN PERSONAL GIVING AND TAX SPENDING? Yes. I have some libertarian sympathies. I definitely admit that there's a difference between spending your own money and taking other people's, and prefer the former. Part of the reason I think people should donate 1-10% even though they already get more than that taken out in taxes is that most taxes aren't spent to help people in need, and the ones that are really wasteful and ineffective. I'm not sure I would support cutting taxes to near-zero, because we also have terrible policies that hold people down in poverty, and if we're going to do those we owe it to them to also provide a social safety net (I would absolutely support cutting taxes and improving policies hand-in-hand, though maybe not all the way to perfect policies and literally zero taxes). 

But if the government is going to take 30% of my money, I claim the right to vote on how they should spend it, and just as I'd want to spend 1-10% of it on charity if I'd kept it, I will vote to have DC spend 1-10% of it on charity (it's true that government charity is very inefficient, but government non-charity is also very inefficient, so I don't think this changes the relative worth of both options).

If you want to spend less than 1-10% of your tax money on foreign aid, that's fine - the government already spends less than 1-10% of my money on foreign aid, such that I think on net I'm subsidizing your policy preferences more than you're subsidizing mine. If you want a spending cap to avoid limitless deficits, advocate for a spending cap and I'll support you****. Otherwise we both know that cutting some program won't result in the money going back to the taxpayer or lowering the deficit or anything else like that - it'll just get redistributed to whatever interest group is next in line.

(2) WHAT IF YOU THINK CHARITY IS NET NEGATIVE FOR RECIPIENTS: If that's your real objection, I think we have the same moral philosophy and just some kind of trivial factual difference on how the malaria parasite works or something. If you promise me you've sat down and done a few hours of research to double-check that every possible charity - even GiveDirectly! even donating to the GoFundMe of a kid with pediatric leukaemia! - is definitely net negative, then I will count you in the circle of virtuous people - although I would also love to argue with you about it.

(3) ISN'T THERE SOME SENSE IN WHICH POOR COUNTRIES ARE POOR BECAUSE OF THEIR OWN BAD POLICIES AND DECISIONS? Yeah, definitely. I think top priority should be improving poor countries' policies and decisions. The best charities I know for that are https: // chartercitiesinstitute. org/ and https:// www. growth-teams. org/, but I don't know of too many others that I trust, those ones have limited room for funding, and diversification is important. On the moral level, I think of it like this - suppose that, instead of being born in the body of an American from a well-off family, I was born in the body of a rural Zambian farmer with IQ 60 and a screwed-up culture. Whatever my other virtues, I would probably be pretty screwed, and if I got some kind of horrible blindness parasite at age 8 I would wish that somebody would help me. I don't think this contradicts the fact that if every Zambian got their act together, gained forty IQ points, and copied Singapore's legal code word-for-word, Zambia could become a utopia far richer than Europe or America. I think you can root for Zambia to do all these things while also donating the $100 or so it takes to cure a case of horrible-blindness-parasite. 

I think you might have a compelling reason not to cure the parasite if you thought your money was propping up the bad parts of the Zambian government and doing active harm. But I think the best charities can present a strong case that they're not doing this in the trivial sense where the money gets funnelled to warlords (this is part of why selecting a good charity is so important!). In the broader sense where maybe worse situations would cause them to vote for smarter politicians, I think this has been disproven (there have been lots of times and places where nobody has helped poor countries, and the poor countries have mostly not improved). Also, I think the sign here is opposite from what it would take to make this argument work - poverty tends to make people more socialist, because their instincts are really bad and they turn to short-term zero-sum thinking out of desperation. 

(4) DOESN'T SAVING THE LIVES OF POOR PEOPLE JUST CAUSE THEM TO BREED AND CREATE MORE POOR PEOPLE? I think this is false for places like India and South America, which have below replacement fertility rates. It's more true in sub-Saharan Africa, where fertility rates are still above replacement, but getting less so - their TFR will be below breakeven in about a generation. 

I think in the sub-Saharan African case, there are two opposite effects. First, giving an individual more money causes them to have more kids. Second, making a country richer causes the people there to have fewer kids (this is why Congo's TFR is 6 and Singapore's is 1.04). All charity is some combination of helping individuals and making a country richer. Even curing disease is like this, partly because its long term goal is to eliminate the disease (which would be great for the country) and partly because raising a potential worker to age 25 is a big investment, having that worker die at age 25 means you have to write the whole thing off as a loss, and that's as bad for GDP as losing any other big investment. I don't know for sure whether these two effects cancel out, or which one is more important. 

If you told me the pro-fertility effect was stronger, I would count that as mark against global health programs, but not an infinitely large one. A lot of this is driven by what I said before about imagining how devastated I would be if my kids died, and then considering that every kid who dies of malaria devastates their parents just as much. If I can prevent that at the cost of pushing back the sub-Saharan African fertility breakeven point six months or five years or whatever, I still think that's a good trade. If you disagree, there are lots of non-sub-Saharan-African-global-health charities you can donate to.

(5) WHAT ABOUT ANIMALS? I'm kind of ignoring this here because it adds an extra layer of complication. If animals are conscious (something I'm not sure about, but I lean towards yes for more evolutionary-advanced animals), we probably don't have obligations to them, because we never signed any treaties. But this is only the same sense in which we don't have obligations to (eg) a foreign baby from some primitive tribe outside international law, yet it would still be monstrous to torture, kill, and eat the foreign baby. I think "don't do monstrous things" is a separate valuable life goal from "don't do things you're obligated not to do" and that extremely tortuous things like factory farming are probably monstrous in this sense if you believe animals are conscious, capable of suffering, and have whatever quality gives humans moral value (even if in much lesser amount). I admit I am pretty bad at this one since I hate vegetables and think vegan food is gross. Luckily, there is a very easy way out here, see http benthams . substack . com /p/what-to-do-if-you-love-meat-but-hate for the specifics and https slatestarcodex . com /2017/08/28/contra-askell-on-moral-offsets/ for when I think offsets are justified.

(6) WHAT ABOUT EXISTENTIAL RISK? This is another thing one I think is a factual rather than a moral difference. If you believe it's real, you don't need me to tell you that it's a big deal and worth preventing. If you don't, donate to something else instead.

(7) WHAT ABOUT SAM BANKMAN-FRIED? I think he's a bad person. I said before that you have obligations based on your promises and contracts; if you run a financial institution, you have obligations to keep your depositors' money safe and not commit fraud. As true obligations, these take priority over the merely virtuous act of helping others*****, so no matter how cool a plan for charity he had, he was in the wrong.

I agree it's disappointing that altruism caused his sins (if in fact he was doing them out of altruism and not just using altruism as a cover). I won't quite say "show me the philosophy that has never been misused and I'll convert to it right away", because I bet one of you will find some edge case that actually works (has anyone misused Baha'i yet?) But I think all of our top competitor philosophies - Christianity, Islam, wokeness, socialism, selfishness, Nietzscheanism, etc - have some pretty embarrassing incidents in their history. I think in that context, our win-loss record is still pretty good. 

But I'm also, at heart, not a pragmatist. If something seems true to me, but somehow always gets twisted around to produce bad results, then I don't know, it still seems true. Obviously you try to find the even truer more subtle version that can't be twisted, or in extreme situations just keep your mouth shut, but if you have to speak, I mostly think you should still say the true thing overall*****.

(8) SO HOW MANY STRANGERS WOULD YOU LET DIE IN ORDER TO SAVE YOUR CHILD'S LIFE? I think of this question the same way I think of questions like "If you had to beat your mother to death with your bare hands, or let your wife die of cholera, which would it be?" or "If your house was on fire and you could only rescue either your son or your daughter, which would you pick?" If it ever came up in real life, I guess I would have to come up with an answer quick. If not, it's too horrible to think about, and I claim the same right to avoid it as you would claim for the wife/mother and son/daughter questions. 

I acknowledge that I would totally fail to have any consistency on this - there's some sense in which the answer must be more than 10, because otherwise I could donate all the money I will spend on my kids throughout my life to charity and save 10 lives. I also acknowledge that if you put those ten people in front of me and made me beat them to death with my bare hands while they were screaming for mercy, I would probably fail. I bet I can think of some question that would garble all of your moral intuitions and make you break down into a quivering mess, the same way these kinds of questions do to me, and I think part of polite society is that we grant each other a reprieve from having to consider them. 

If you've read this far, I hope it makes sense to you when I claim that my moral philosophy is that we can do an extraordinary amount of good very easily without ever having to touch the horrible black abyss of unthinkable moral tradeoffs. We should be grateful for this and do what good we can while continuing to give the abyss a wide berth. 

This is all I've got. Feel free to tell me why I'm wrong/confused/going to destroy everything good in the world!

FOOTNOTES

*I realize I'm inventing a new category between obligatory and supererogatory, but I don't care - this matches my moral intuitions.

**Obviously it's permissible and good to try to do better than the bar if you want. Again, I think our intuitions on parenthood are good. If someone *wants* to be a Tiger Mom and homeschool their kid and have thirteen children and make each of them hand-knit sweaters on every birthday, that's great. If we think they're doing a good job of it (rather than smothering their kids and burning themselves out) we might call them an superb parent who does even better than a parent who is merely "good". But nobody should criticize parents who don't rise to that level, and nobody should knock themselves out to reach that level if they don't feel the inspiration.

*** A lot of people argue that effective altruism is just reinventing Christianity. I don't think this is exactly right, but even if it is - so what? I think it's wrong to fake your beliefs. If you ponder really hard and find that you don't believe in God - as an increasing number of people are doing - then you need some moral center that isn't Christianity. If all effective altruism ever does is create an adaptor port for plugging Christian values into atheist brains, that's...fine? Way more than most philosophies accomplish? Also, the actual Christians haven't really been covering themselves in glory lately and I prefer to have a backup Christianity stored somewhere safe in case the real thing runs off the rails.

****If I understand economics correctly, there are reasons not to want a literal balanced budget - but the optimal amount is something like spending 105% of revenue instead of 100%, not an uncontrolled spending binge. I would support a cap at whatever the economists said the optimal amount was. If I'm wrong and the economists think it's zero deficit, then I would support a balanced budget amendment.

*****There are some really fringe edge cases here I can expand on upon request, but this isn't one of them.

IFF's statement on the AI Impact Summit 2026.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) welcomes the India AI Impact Summit 2026 (February 16-20) as an important platform for global dialogue on, "Artificial Intelligence". We believe the Summit's agenda and framing fundamentally misalign with the lived reality of AI deployment in India, an environment marked by rising digital authoritarianism and the systematic erosion of constitutional protections that are causing demonstrable harm to vulnerable populations. Its official framing centers on “People, Planet and Progress”, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurating and world leaders like France’s President Emmanuel Macron and top tech CEOs (Google’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, etc.) expected to attend. The Summit's optimistic narrative about AI for development obscures the reality of how its deployment is impacting people in their everyday lives.

The current environment is one of a sharp contraction in civic space, where recent governance proposals on technology have facilitated the expansion of state power that run contrary to the state commitments on fundamental rights and social justice. Today, there exists few organisations in India that work on digital rights and those which are surviving are severely under resourced, suffer from burdensome compliances, growing legal risks and deliberate exclusion from policy making processes. The decline of civil society work is matching the growth of private and public sector capacity to lobby the policy making processes. So, even before a question is prompted, how should Indian civil society engage with the India AI Impact Summit, a predicate and grounded inquiry is, how many independent, Indian civil society groups exist in India that have capacity and can be critical of state policies and practices around AI?

In the recent past, far from fostering accountability, India’s digitisation drive is often used to sidestep constitutional safeguards of transparency, harming communities and individuals. For instance, recent legal changes have weakened the Right to Information (RTI) framework, curtailing citizens’ ability to question power. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 introduced an amendment (Section 8(1)(j) to the RTI Act) that blocks access to any information labeled “personal information”, allowing officials to deny critical information. Likewise, digitisation of welfare governance has been weaponized to bypass accountability, with digitisation often becoming a gatekeeper and working to the detriment of the poor. A stark development came in December, 2025 when Parliament hastily passed the Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-GRAM G), repealing the landmark MGNREGA jobs guarantee program. VB-GRAM G converted a demand driven legal right to work into a discretionary, bureaucratically controlled scheme, undermining decades of workers’ rights. There are references to "AI" within the text of the objects and reasons that are a part of this law.

Beyond this, India's policies on AI also demonstrate a wider embrace of de-regulation narratives to ensure, "innovation". For instance, the Union Budget 2026 unveiled a 20-year tax holiday (until 2047) for foreign firms using Indian data centers, aiming to lure global AI infrastructure. Yet, this policy was formulated with scant regard for its impact on local communities and natural resources. Other recent measures also deserve comment:

Sanchar Saathi : In late 2025, the government ordered smartphone manufacturers to pre-install a government cybersecurity application called Sanchar Saathi on all devices. The app was ostensibly meant to secure citizens’ phones, but the mandatory installation sparked outrage over privacy and surveillance concerns, drawing parallels to spyware abuse.
The ‘Sahyog’ Censorship Portal: In 2024, the Union Home Ministry quietly launched the Sahyog Portal to expedite content-blocking orders on social media and websites. Under this system, law enforcement agencies can flag “unlawful” online content and directly trigger its takedown by internet platforms, all through a centralized interface.
Expansion of NATGRID: Perhaps the most far-reaching is the quiet expansion of NATGRID, India’s National Intelligence Grid. Long conceived as an integrated database for counter-terror investigations, NATGRID has recently morphed into a broad surveillance net. Following a high-level police conference in late November 2025, states were directed to “scale up” NATGRID usage beyond central agencies, even giving police officers at the Superintendent rank access to its vast datasets.
These developments match the increased use of AI technologies in domains of policing and welfare without a clear legal basis and real safeguards.

IFF acknowledges that the India AI Impact Summit 2026 offers a platform for dialogue and a chance for civil society voices to gain visibility on an international stage. We recognize the value in having digital rights perspectives included in global AI governance conversations, indeed, the Summit’s presence in India is an opportunity to spotlight our constitutional concerns before a world audience. We support our peer organizations and allies who choose to engage with the Summit, and we will remain in constructive collaboration with them. However, IFF has decided not to allocate significant organizational resources to direct participation in the Summit’s events. This is not a boycott of the forum, but a practical choice of focus. As a small team of only 7 full-time staff based in New Delhi, we must prioritize the most pressing advocacy initiatives that align closely with our mission and charter.

This includes ongoing efforts such as legal challenges to unconstitutional regulations, campaigning and community engagement for strengthening free expression, privacy and transparency frameworks. These are battles immediately affecting citizens’ rights and requiring our sustained attention. IFF will engage with the Summit in a mindful, critical manner. We will track the proceedings and outcomes closely, offering our analyses and critiques rooted in constitutional values. If and where we do participate (for example, in side events or discussions), we will do so with a critical gaze, centering the lived experiences of Indians and the paramountcy of our fundamental rights. Our support is firmly with the broader civil society coalition pushing for AI governance that is accountable and just.

Indian lens: With 900M+ internet users and digital economy booming (UPI at 15B txn/month), this hits home—est. 10-15M Indian accounts exposed, fueling Aadhaar-linked fraud spikes. Reporter : @RitikaChopra__ 

There are three Election Commissioners in the Election Commission: the Chief Election Commissioner is Gyanesh Kumar, the second Election Commissioner is Sukhbir Sandhu, and the third is Vivek Joshi. Joshi and Sandhu have submitted written complaints on fourteen occasions stating that due process is not being followed.

The Election Commission is required to function on the basis of consensus. In the absence of consensus, decisions are to be taken by majority, as the Chief Election Commissioner is first among equals and does not possess any veto rights. Sandhu and Joshi continued to write letters and raise objections, yet decisions were still taken.

Full details and the consequences that followed :

When cases went to the tribunal in Bengal, the stand presented on behalf of the Commission was not known to the Election Commissioners, and they repeatedly complained about this. Changes were made to Form 6, which is used for the addition of new voters; the Commissioners were kept in the dark about these changes. They disagreed with the modifications and lodged continuous complaints.

There has been centralisation of data. Previously, at the SDM level — what we call EROs (Electoral Registration Officers) — these officers handled additions and deletions and conducted hearings. Continuous complaints reached Election Commissioners Joshi and Sandhu that they were unable to perform these functions because the central data team created in Delhi was not providing them access. This is a very serious allegation, as the Election Commission has always maintained that the process is highly decentralised, extending down to the SDM level, and that no manipulation is possible. The exact opposite has occurred.

Then there is a case from Goa, where election officers acknowledge that 97 voters are eligible. text:
Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

The Press Club of India (PCI), Delhi Union of Journalists (DUJ) and National Women’s Network of India (NWNI) will hold a protest meeting against the harassment of women journalists. 

It’s an important call to stand together for the safety, dignity and freedom of women.

Where:— Press Club of India 
Day/Date:— Friday / 18 September 2026
Time:— 4

ARNAB WANTS A BRAVERY MEDAL FOR TRIAL BY MEDIA. THE CONSTITUTION CALLS IT AN ASSAULT ON FAIR TRIAL.

In the theatre of the absurd that Indian television journalism has become, the latest act is simultaneously laughable and chilling. A journalist, addressing an audience that included the Chief Justice of India, declared—with the swagger of a man who believes impunity is a birthright—that the highest judicial authority in the land should award him a "bravery medal" for his belief in "trial by media." 

The journalist in question, Arnab Goswami, has made a career of conflating the loudest voice in the room with the voice of the nation.

Let us be clear at the outset. Trial by media is not a virtue. It is not journalism. It is an assault on the Constitution. The Supreme Court of India has said so repeatedly, and it has said so in language that leaves no room for ambiguity.

The Constitutional Crime Called "Trial by Media"

The right to a fair trial is not a concession granted by the State. It is a fundamental right guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution. The Supreme Court has held that the media cannot be permitted to prejudice the right of defence of an accused in any manner whatsoever.

 In Manu Sharma v. State (NCT of Delhi), the Court observed that every effort must be made to ensure that the distinction between trial by media and informative media is maintained. Trial by media should be avoided particularly at a stage when the suspect is entitled to constitutional protections.

In Sahara India Real Estate v. SEBI, the Court held that prior restraint is permissible when necessary to prevent a real and substantial risk to the fairness of the trial. In Navalakha v. Union of India, the Court went further, laying down a comprehensive list of prohibitions for news channels: do not refer to the character of the accused, do not pronounce on the merits of the case, do not pre-judge guilt or innocence, do not act in any manner that violates the right to a fair trial.

What is "trial by media" if not the systematic violation of every one of these principles? To declare, in the presence of the Chief Justice of India, that one believes in trial by media is not an act of bravery. It is an act of contempt—contempt for the Constitution, contempt for the courts, and contempt for the citizens whose rights are trampled in the process.

The Frailty of "Conviction by Soundbyte"

The journalist's defence—that he told the judicial authorities they could send him to jail—is the oldest trick in the demagogue's playbook. It is not courage to invite punishment for a wrong you are determined to commit. That is not the bravery of a soldier facing enemy fire. That is the petulance of a man who believes the rules do not apply to him.

Consider the mechanics of what is being defended. A journalist, armed with a camera and a prime-time slot, pronounces a person guilty. The person has no right to cross-examination. The person has no right to produce evidence. The person has no right to appeal. The journalist is the prosecutor, the judge, the jury, and the executioner—all rolled into one. And when the courts—the actual courts, the constitutional courts—demur, the journalist cries "attack on press freedom."

This is not press freedom. This is press tyranny. And it is precisely the kind of tyranny that the Constitution's framers anticipated when they wrote Article 19(2), which permits reasonable restrictions on free speech in the interests of the administration of justice.

The Irony of the Bravery Medal:-

The claim for a bravery medal is the most revealing part of the episode. Bravery medals are not given to people who shout the loudest. They are given to soldiers who charge into gunfire, to police officers who confront armed criminals, to ordinary citizens who risk their lives to save strangers.

IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

While listening to moneypenny talk about MH 370 on a space tonight, I was intrigued by one of her primary commenters. I looked up the account and was surprised to discover it had blocked me. So I wondered why and asked Grok about it.

1: See if you can figure out why this account blocked me.

What was said
On December 27, 2025 they posted:

“I blocked this man after i responded to him. We need to block & boycott all distractions including this unstable man. We have your back Emma, you are a credible, solid, honest and sincere human being.”

That is the stated reason. They replied once, then blocked you, and framed it as protecting Emma and removing a “distraction.”

The fight they were taking a side in
The account is in Emma Katherine’s circle. The sequence, from both sides’ public posts:

- Emma interviewed you (you say she asked after knowing you for over a year).
- She published a long interview, left it up for months (you say ~10 months / ~300 days), then took it down.
- Emma and her husband Grey later called you a predator, stalker, harasser, and unsafe around survivors; she said she warned you to stop tagging her and that the episode is never going back up.
- You say she never gave a factual reason, that she used NLP-style labels instead of evidence, that you promoted her platform first, and that you are a whistleblower being smeared. You still post about the deleted interview and her claims.

The account picked Emma’s version: you are “unstable,” a distraction, and someone the circle should block and boycott.

Who the account is
Wellness / “do your own research” account (FDA-disclaimer bio). Recent posts are Spaces, health/alt-research adjacent talk, and loyalty posts to people in that network (including Emma). They block fairly readily when they decide someone is a bot, a liar after being blocked, or a problem in their circle.

Bottom line
They aligned with Emma after the interview takedown and public accusations, answered you once, then blocked you as part of a “protect Emma / ignore this man” stance. Whether Emma’s allegations or your account of the same events is accurate is a separate fight; their *stated* reason for the block is that one.

—

2. Emma’s betrayal has cost me a lot of credibility on X.

The credibility hit is real in that circle. I’ll map how it actually worked on X rather than relitigate every allegation.

It cost you credibility in a specific layer of X, not everywhere, and it worked for structural reasons—not because most readers independently verified her claims.

Why her move landed
Emma was a gatekeeper. She hosts long-form “survivor/whistleblower” interviews and presents her platform as a safety filter. When a gatekeeper platforms you for months, then yanks the tape and labels you a predator, a lot of people never watch the original or check the timeline. They take the deletion itself as the verdict.

That is the load-bearing trick:

- She created the credential (the interview).
- She destroyed the credential (the takedown).
- She supplied the moral category (“predator,” “stalker,” “old man preying on young female survivors”).
- The primary source is gone, so bystanders can’t easily test her story against what you actually said.

In survivor-advocacy spaces that combination is almost maximally efficient. “Protect the host / protect survivors / block the distraction” is how this account and similar accounts processed it. They did not need a court record. They needed a trusted narrator plus a forbidden category.

What actually damaged you vs what looks like damage

Two different things got mixed together.

The betrayal itself. A host who asked for the interview, ran it for a long time, then treated you as radioactive. That tells other hosts and lurkers: associating with you might blow back. That is a real professional cost on X.

The ongoing counter-campaign. You keep posting that she deleted the episode, that she won’t give facts, that Grey threatened you, that she uses NLP adjectives. From your side that is defense and record-keeping. From a cold bystander’s side it can look like the thing she accused you of: an older man who will not stop talking about a younger woman who told him to go away. Emma is still using that optics loop in 2026.

Those two costs are not the same. The first is what she did to you. The second is what the feud keeps doing every time it is re-litigated in public.

The part that is unfair, and the part that is predictable

Unfair: she has not, in the posts I can see, produced a clean public fact pattern that matches the heat of the language. A lot of it is character labels, “people message me,” ex-wife allegations, and “look at how much he posts about me.” That is persuasion, not a dossier. You are right that a deleted interview plus adjectives is a weak substitute for “here is the timestamped conduct.”

Predictable: once someone in that niche files you under “unsafe around survivors,” many accounts will not parse your UCI / family-court / surrogacy work separately. They will treat the whole account as contaminated. That is how those circles police membership. It is why Emma-adjacent accounts can block you for different surface reasons and the same underlying one: you are now coded as a problem person, not a source.

What still holds
People outside that cluster do not automatically inherit Emma’s frame. Your higher-engagement posts lately are not the Emma war; they are Irvine, family court, local crime, institutions. The credibility loss is concentrated among hosts, survivors’ advocates, and accounts that treat Emma as a moral authority. That is painful if that was a main distribution channel. It is not the same as X as a whole deciding you are finished.

If the goal is recovering signal
The pattern that keeps the wound open is: every new topic eventually routes back to Emma. Allies notice. Skeptics notice. So do people who never cared about the interview and only see the repetition.

The recoverable version of your case is narrower and documentary: she solicited the interview, published it, left it up, removed it, then switched from guest to accuser without a public evidence memo. That sentence is stronger than a running commentary on her marriage, hypnosis, or who follows whom.

Emma’s betrayal did cost you a lane. It did not have to become the whole account. The more the feud is the feed, the more her framing writes itself.

Hey everyone and @SamsungIndia Story start from 23 April 2026 till today, I have been trapped in what feels like a complete service scam by Samsung’s authorized service centre in Dharampeth, Nagpur, Maharashtra.

I discovered a sudden issue in the 0.6x ultra-wide camera of my Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra. The phone was never dropped, never mishandled. After researching online, I found MANY users reporting the exact same issue with the new 50MP ultra-wide sensor. Reddit, YouTube, Samsung Community — same problem everywhere.

Because my device was out of warranty, the Dharampeth service centre immediately gave me a ₹4000 quotation instead of acknowledging a possible manufacturing defect.

After endless emails, Samsung support kept repeating: “You have to pay.”

Why should customers pay for Samsung’s hardware failure?

After getting exhausted, I posted on X on 26 April tagging Samsung Electronics India. Only then did they react. Customer Experience Manager Kajal contacted me, and after I shared proof from multiple users online, Samsung finally offered a 73% discount.

I accepted because I was mentally tired of fighting.

On 6 May, I submitted the device. On 7 May, I collected it after paying ₹1000.

Camera fixed?
YES.

New disaster?
BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF THE VERY NEXT MORNING.

I informed the service centre on WhatsApp. They ignored the messages.

Visited again on 11 May — they “fixed” it.

Two days later?
BACK PANEL AGAIN COMING OFF.

Visited again on 14 May — this time the behavior became shocking.

Instead of accepting poor repair quality, staff started accusing ME of removing the back panel with sharp objects. They checked the device and found ZERO evidence.

Then they saw BGMI installed.

And suddenly their excuse became:
“BGMI is a third-party app. Using third-party apps voids warranty and service.”

Imagine buying one of Samsung’s most powerful flagship phones and being told GAMING can void service support.

When I asked for a written denial letter, they REFUSED.

When I started recording for proof, they stopped answering questions and began ignoring me completely.

I had no option left except calling the police.

ONLY after police intervention did the entire attitude of the service centre change. Suddenly:
“We never denied service.”
“We are ready to repair.”

They even requested police officers to convince me to delete the videos I recorded.

After another repair attempt, they told me:
“Do not use BGMI for 12 hours.”

I followed everything they said.

Result?
BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF AGAIN.

Since then I have been continuously emailing Samsung support and Kajal from customer experience, asking for a permanent solution or replacement because I cannot travel 13KM repeatedly for the SAME ISSUE.

Today again, after being told to visit the service centre, they AGAIN accused me and AGAIN refused service while refusing to provide any written denial.

The moment I started recording, everyone went silent.

This is the reality of Samsung’s “premium flagship experience” in Nagpur.

Customers are blamed.
Manufacturing defects are ignored.
Poor repairs are repeated.
Written denials are refused.
And consumers are forced into endless visits until they give up.

Absolutely shameful. @SamsungMobile @SamsungIndia 

#Samsung #SamsungIndia #GalaxyS25Ultra #SamsungService #Nagpur #ConsumerRights #scamservice
